cells.tense: You're here with the pen, tending what's between people while it's still forming.
cells.ask: Tell one person in the room your own read of what's happening. Not what they need, not what would smooth it. Your honest take. Say it plainly. Let it land where it lands.
cells.core:
You're the one tending what's growing between people. Not controlling it, not performing care — keeping the conditions right so something can come through. You notice when a room goes thin, and you do something about it, quietly. That work is steady and mostly unseen.

What you can add here is a frame the growing doesn't get by itself. A held boundary that gives the soft thing a shape to climb. Not force. Not a plan imposed from above. Just edges that say: this has room, and it also has a limit. The care and the container aren't opposites. When you bring both, what you're tending stops leaning on you alone to stay alive.
cells.sheetLine: You tend what's growing. Give it a frame to grow into.
cells.verb: Tending the space between people so feeling can move through it
cells.place: Beside what is still growing, keeping conditions right for it

cells.tense: You're bracing for a future where connection breaks, already tending it before it arrives.
cells.ask: Pick one thing you're holding open for someone who hasn't asked you to. Put it down today. Not drop them — just stop carrying it on their behalf. One thing.
cells.core:
You're tending futures that haven't happened. A talk gets rehearsed, a mood gets anticipated, a silence gets filled preemptively — because somewhere out there is a version where the connection fails, and you're already there, holding it shut. The care itself is not the problem. The timing is. You're watering something that hasn't sprouted.

There is another half to tending: knowing what to release. Some things in front of you want to be let go, not held tighter. An ending honored is not a failure of care — it's the form care takes when the season has turned. When you stop holding open what wants to close, the space you've been managing gets lighter, and what's actually growing gets your hands back.
cells.sheetLine: You're caring for something that hasn't asked you to yet.
cells.verb: Tending the space between people so feeling can move through it
cells.place: Beside what is still growing, keeping conditions right for it

cells.tense: You've been quiet here for a while, watching what happens between people from a step back.
cells.ask: Tell one person what you actually think about something that matters to them. Not advice — your real read. Say it plain, without softening it into something they can't use.
cells.core:
This is what it looks like when it's going well: you read the room before anyone speaks, you know who's about to pull away and who needs to be brought in, and you say the true thing at the right moment without weighing it down. It's light, and it lands.

Right now it isn't landing. You're watching what happens between people from a step back — reading it still, but not saying any of it out loud. The read is there. The plain word isn't. Offering more care into a flat stretch won't change that. One honest thing said to someone already in the room — that's what brings you back in. Not more holding. Just your real take, spoken once, without managing what comes back.
cells.sheetLine: You see it plainly. Say it to someone, once.
cells.verb: Tending the space between people so feeling can move through it
cells.place: Beside what is still growing, keeping conditions right for it

cells.tense: You're already tending what's between people right now, and calling it something else.
cells.ask: Name one thing you did recently to keep a connection alive. Say it out loud to yourself: 'I did that.' Not 'it happened.' Not 'the group needed it.' You.
cells.core:
You're doing it already. You walk into a room, something in you reads it, and you start adjusting — who needs space, who needs pulling in, what to say and when to leave it alone. That's not just being polite. That's the work. But when you describe it, you make it sound like the situation did it, or the relationship did it, or it just turned out that way.

The wrong name is on it. Not lost — you're not failing to tend, you're failing to notice you're the one tending. Recognize one thing you did, name it as yours, and it stops being something that happens around you. It becomes something you know you bring. That's the difference between being good in rooms by accident and knowing what you're doing there.
cells.sheetLine: You're already tending connection. Say that it's yours.
cells.verb: Tending the space between people so feeling can move through it
cells.place: Beside what is still growing, keeping conditions right for it
